708.title: Gleaning (Ruth 2)
708.hook: Ruth gathers leftover grain, and Boaz tells his workers to drop some on purpose
708.howItsDone: Christians read Ruth 2 together with the gleaning laws of Leviticus and Deuteronomy, and some churches and charities name food-rescue work, gathering surplus harvest for people in need, after gleaning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Naomi, who came home calling herself Mara. Your line was where you go, I go.

Barley harvest in Bethlehem. Two widows have come home with nothing to eat, and the younger one makes a plan: "Let me now go to the field, and glean ears of corn." To glean is to walk behind the reapers and pick up what they drop: stray stalks, the bits at the edges. So Ruth, a foreigner, goes out alone. And the storyteller says, almost with a wink, "her hap was to light on a part of the field belonging unto Boaz," a relative of Naomi's dead husband. Then Boaz walks out from town and greets his workers, "The LORD be with you," and they answer, "The LORD bless thee."
screen: `LET ME NOW GO TO THE FIELD.`
`HER HAP WAS TO LIGHT ON BOAZ'S FIELD.`

segments.voice: Ruth isn't begging. She's using a law. In Leviticus, God tells Israel: "thou shalt not wholly reap the corners of thy field, neither shalt thou gather the gleanings of thy harvest." Leave them for the poor and the stranger. Deuteronomy adds the forgotten sheaf: don't go back for it; "it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow." Ruth is two of those three at once. The law built a margin into every farm, so the hungry could feed themselves with their own hands. Boaz notices her. He tells her to stay in his field, and that his young men won't touch her. Ruth falls on her face: "Why have I found grace in thine eyes, that thou shouldest take knowledge of me, seeing I am a stranger?" He's heard what she did for Naomi, and he blesses her under the God of Israel, "under whose wings thou art come to trust." As she gets up to glean, Boaz quietly tells his reapers: "let fall also some of the handfuls of purpose for her, and leave them, that she may glean them, and rebuke her not." The law said leave the edges and what drops. Boaz goes past it: drop more, on purpose, and say nothing. That evening she beats out what she gathered, and the text says it was about an ephah of barley. Hearing the name Boaz, the bitter widow from yesterday says, "Blessed be he of the LORD, who hath not left off his kindness to the living and to the dead."
screen: `THE LAW LEFT THE EDGES FOR STRANGERS.`
`WHY ME, SEEING I AM A STRANGER?`

segments.voice: Look through the rest of your day for the edges of your field: a little extra time, money, food or attention, the last slice. Pick one thing you could leave quietly for someone, so they simply find it, the way Ruth found the handfuls: no speech, no credit. If you pray, hold that person in prayer as you decide.
Gleaning. Gathering what the reapers leave behind. The law left the edges of the field for the poor and the stranger, and Boaz left more.
Your line: drop some on purpose. A kindness that lets someone simply find it. Day seven hundred eight, done.

709.title: Grandmother of a king (Ruth 4)
709.hook: an immigrant widow becomes great-grandmother of David, in Jesus' family tree
709.howItsDone: Christians read the end of Ruth together with Matthew 1, where Ruth is named in the family line of Jesus, as part of the story of how God's people came to include those from outside it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gleaning: Boaz let some fall on purpose. Your line was drop some on purpose.

A man sits down at the city gate and waits. Here the gate works like a courthouse. In chapter three, Naomi sends Ruth to the threshing floor, and Ruth asks Boaz to spread his skirt over her, "for thou art a near kinsman." She's asking him to marry her, and to take up the family's cause. Boaz says yes, with one problem: there's a closer relative. In the morning the closer relative walks past the gate, and Boaz calls out, "Ho, such a one! turn aside, sit down here." Ten elders sit down to watch.
screen: `HO, SUCH A ONE! SIT DOWN HERE.`

segments.voice: The Hebrew word for this relative is go'el, a redeemer: the near kinsman whose duty is to buy back family land and keep a dead man's name alive. Naomi has a field to sell. Will you redeem it? I will, says the man. Then Boaz adds: the day you buy the field, you also take Ruth the Moabitess, the dead man's widow. The man backs out: "I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I mar mine own inheritance." He passes his shoe to Boaz, the old way of sealing a deal, and the man with no name walks out of the Bible. Boaz marries Ruth, and they have a son. The last words go to the women of the town, speaking to Naomi. In chapter one she came home empty. Now they say this child will restore her life and nourish her old age, "for thy daughter in law, which loveth thee, which is better to thee than seven sons, hath born him." Better than seven sons, said of a foreign daughter-in-law. Naomi lays the boy in her bosom, and the neighbors name him Obed. Then the book widens in one sentence: "he is the father of Jesse, the father of David." The Moabite widow who gleaned in a stranger's field is the great-grandmother of Israel's king. Matthew's family line of Jesus names her too: "Booz begat Obed of Ruth." The genealogy could have listed only fathers. It stops to say her name. Some readers take that as a sign the outsider was in the story all along.
screen: `THE MAN WITH NO NAME BACKS OUT.`

segments.voice: Go back through your own line, or your town, to someone who came from somewhere else: a grandparent who crossed a border, a neighbor who learned your language, someone who married into the family and was never quite treated as family. Let one of them come to mind, and name one thing you have because they came. If you pray, give thanks for them.
Go'el, Hebrew for a redeemer: the near kinsman who buys back family land and keeps a dead man's name alive, as Boaz did.
Your line: the outsider in the line. A Moabite widow, in a king's family. That's day seven hundred nine.

710.title: Hannah's prayer (1 Samuel 1)
710.hook: a woman prays so hard the priest thinks she's drunk
710.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Hannah's story when they pray about longing, infertility or grief, and read her silent prayer in 1 Samuel 1 alongside her song of thanks in 1 Samuel 2.

segments.voice: Yesterday, go'el, the redeemer. Your line was the outsider in the line.

"How long wilt thou be drunken? put away thy wine from thee." That's a priest, speaking to a woman at prayer. His name is Eli, and he's sitting by a post of the temple of the LORD at Shiloh, watching her. Her lips are moving. No sound comes out. So he decides she's had too much at the family's meal. He couldn't be more wrong. The first book of Samuel doesn't open with a king or a battle. It opens with a woman who can't have children, a family trip to worship, and a prayer so deep it looks like a scandal.

Back up. Hannah's husband, Elkanah, has two wives. "Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children." Every year at Shiloh, the text says, her rival provoked her sore, until Hannah wept and couldn't eat. Elkanah loves her, and tries: "Hannah, why weepest thou? and why eatest thou not? and why is thy heart grieved? am not I better to thee than ten sons?" Yesterday the women told Naomi that Ruth was better than seven sons. Here a husband asks if he's better than ten, and the text gives no answer from her. Hannah gets up and goes to pray. "She was in bitterness of soul, and prayed unto the LORD, and wept sore." She vows: if God will remember her and give her a son, she'll give him back to the LORD all his life. Then: "Hannah, she spake in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard: therefore Eli thought she had been drunken." When he scolds her, she doesn't flinch. "No, my lord, I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit: I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but have poured out my soul before the LORD." Poured out, like water from a jar, nothing kept back. Eli changes his mind at once: "Go in peace," and may God grant your petition. And here's the detail to carry: Hannah goes and eats, and "her countenance was no more sad." She isn't pregnant yet. Nothing has changed. Only the jar is empty. Later she has a son and names him Samuel, "Because I have asked him of the LORD." And she keeps her vow.
screen: `AM NOT I BETTER TO THEE THAN TEN SONS?`

segments.voice: Let whatever's heaviest come up, the thing you want and don't have, the thing that keeps hurting, without shaping it into sentences; Hannah's voice wasn't heard. Let your breath carry it out slowly, like tipping a jar until it's empty, and notice what's left. If you pray, do this before God.
Hannah's prayer. A silent prayer at Shiloh, so deep the priest thought she was drunk. She poured out her soul before the LORD, and went home no more sad.
Your line: poured out before the lord. Her face changed before anything else did. See you tomorrow.

711.title: Speak, Lord (1 Samuel 3)
711.hook: a boy hears his name at night three times, and finally answers
711.carry: let none of his words fall to the ground
711.howItsDone: Some Christians use Samuel's words, speak, for thy servant heareth, before reading scripture or in quiet prayer, and read 1 Samuel 3 as a story about learning to recognize God's call.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hannah's prayer, and your line was poured out before the lord.

"And the word of the LORD was precious in those days; there was no open vision." Precious here means rare. Heaven had gone quiet. Hannah's son Samuel is now a boy serving the old priest Eli at Shiloh, and one night he's lying down in the temple, where the ark of God is. The lamp of God hasn't gone out yet. Eli's eyes have grown so dim he can't see. Then a voice calls the boy's name. He runs to the old man: "Here am I; for thou calledst me." Eli sends him back to bed. It happens a second time, and a third.
screen: `THE LAMP OF GOD NOT YET OUT.`
`HERE AM I; FOR THOU CALLEDST ME.`

segments.voice: Why does Samuel keep running to the wrong room? The text answers plainly: "Now Samuel did not yet know the LORD, neither was the word of the LORD yet revealed unto him." He's never heard this voice, so he takes it for the one voice he knows: Eli's. On the third time, the old man who can barely see is the one who perceives it: "Eli perceived that the LORD had called the child." Eli hasn't restrained his own sons, a scandal in the chapter before. But tonight he does the one thing a teacher can do. He gives the boy words: if he calls you, "thou shalt say, Speak, LORD; for thy servant heareth." The LORD comes and calls as before, and the boy answers, "Speak; for thy servant heareth." He leaves one word out. Eli said Speak, LORD. Samuel says only Speak. Some readers have wondered why: nerves, not yet knowing the name, or the text being careful. It doesn't say. What comes next is hard: a message of judgment on Eli's own house. In the morning Samuel is afraid to tell him. Eli insists, and when he hears it, says only, "It is the LORD: let him do what seemeth him good." Then the chapter closes on the boy: the LORD was with him, and let none of his words fall to the ground. A quiet season ends with a child who learned to answer, from a man who knew he was being passed over.
screen: `SAMUEL DID NOT YET KNOW THE LORD.`
`A HARD WORD FOR ELI'S OWN HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Samuel kept answering the voice he already knew, so for a moment set aside the usual voices in your head: the list, the worry, the old arguments. If you pray, say the boy's words once, quietly, "Speak; for thy servant heareth," and then stop talking; if you don't, simply say to yourself, I'm listening, and let the quiet stay quiet. Don't hunt for a message; just practice being the one who hears.
Speak. The boy Samuel's answer in the night at Shiloh, after three calls and an old priest's help: speak; for thy servant heareth.
Your line: let none of his words fall to the ground. Day seven hundred eleven, done.

712.title: Give us a king (1 Samuel 8)
712.hook: the people want a king like everyone else, and are warned what kings take
712.howItsDone: Christians read 1 Samuel 8 in different ways, as a warning about power and as part of the long road to King David, and some read it when thinking about how much to borrow from the culture around them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, speak, and your line: let none of his words fall to the ground.
screen: `LET NONE OF HIS WORDS FALL TO THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: The boy who answered in the night is an old man now, and the story repeats in a way that stings. Samuel makes his sons judges, and "his sons walked not in his ways, but turned aside after lucre, and took bribes, and perverted judgment." Eli's sons all over again. So the elders of Israel come to Samuel at Ramah with a reasonable request: you're old, your sons aren't like you, "now make us a king to judge us like all the nations." And the text says, simply, "the thing displeased Samuel."
screen: `HIS SONS WALKED NOT IN HIS WAYS.`

segments.voice: Samuel prays, and God's answer surprises twice. First: give them what they ask. "Hearken unto the voice of the people in all that they say unto thee: for they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them." It isn't about you, Samuel. Second: warn them first. Samuel's speech is blunt, and its key word is take. "He will take your sons" for his chariots, his horsemen, his fields, his weapons. "He will take your daughters to be confectionaries, and to be cooks, and to be bakers." Your best fields, a tenth of your grain and flocks, your servants, your donkeys. "And ye shall be his servants." One day you'll cry out because of the king you chose. The people don't argue with a single point: "Nay; but we will have a king over us; That we also may be like all the nations; and that our king may judge us, and go out before us, and fight our battles." Like all the nations, again. They heard every cost and still chose to belong. God tells Samuel, make them a king. Readers hear this chapter more than one way. Some hear a warning against kingship itself, or against any power that only takes. Others point out that Deuteronomy had already allowed for a king, and that the trouble was the reason: to be like everyone else. Christian readers also follow this road on to David and a promised throne, and to Jesus called the son of David. The chapter ends with the request granted, and the warning on the record.
screen: `NAY; BUT WE WILL HAVE A KING.`
`READERS HEAR IT MORE THAN ONE WAY.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you want right now mostly because others have it: a phone, a look, a kind of house, a stance online. Don't judge it yet; just ask Samuel's question, what will it take, and let the list come: your time, your money, your attention, your quiet. If you pray, bring that wanting to God as it is.
Ramah. The town where Israel's elders came to Samuel and asked for a king to judge and lead them like all the nations, after hearing everything a king would take.
Your line: not like the nations. Belonging can cost more than it appears. See you tomorrow.

713.title: Hiding among the baggage (1 Samuel 10:17–24)
713.hook: chosen as king, tall Saul hides among the luggage
713.tomorrow: The Lord looks on the heart
713.howItsDone: Christians read Saul's hiding as a very human moment at the start of a story that ends in tragedy, and preachers sometimes use it to talk about the fear that comes with being called.

segments.voice: Yesterday, at Ramah, the elders said give us a king. Your line was not like the nations.

The whole nation is gathered at Mizpeh to find out who their king will be, and they're choosing by lot. Tribe by tribe, the lot narrows. The tribe of Benjamin is taken. Then one family in Benjamin. Then one man: Saul, the son of Kish. Every head turns. And the text says, "when they sought him, he could not be found." The king is missing from his own coronation. So they enquire of the LORD further: where is he? And the answer comes back, in the King James words: "Behold, he hath hid himself among the stuff."

The stuff is the baggage: the gear and supplies people brought to the gathering. Somewhere behind the packs, the new king is crouching. And he's not easy to hide. When they fetch him and he stands up, "he was higher than any of the people from his shoulders and upward." Taller than everyone, folded up behind the luggage. Why hide? The story has given clues. In the chapter before, Saul was out looking for his father's lost donkeys when he met Samuel. Samuel told him the desire of all Israel was on him, and Saul answered, "Am not I a Benjamite, of the smallest of the tribes of Israel?" Then Samuel anointed him in private with a vial of oil. So when the lot falls, Saul has already been anointed, and he hides anyway. Fear, modesty, dread of the weight: the text doesn't say which, and readers have heard all three. Samuel presents him: "See ye him whom the LORD hath chosen, that there is none like him among all the people?" And the people shout, "God save the king." One more detail, just past today's verses. Not everyone cheers. Some say, how shall this man save us, and they despise him and bring him no gifts. "But he held his peace." Some readers who know how Saul's story ends come back to this chapter, to the tall, frightened man behind the bags, before anything went wrong.
screen: `THE STUFF: THE GEAR AND THE BAGS.`

segments.voice: Ask where you're hiding among the stuff right now: a role you keep dodging, a conversation that's yours to have, a gift tucked behind busyness or being too tired. Let one come to mind, and without stepping out yet, picture standing up from behind the bags, all the way up. If you pray, ask for courage to be found.
Mizpeh. The gathering place where Saul, chosen by lot, hid himself among the stuff, and had to be fetched out to stand before the people.
Your line: come out from the baggage. Even a king, already anointed, can hide. Day seven hundred thirteen, done.

714.title: The Lord looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:1–13)
714.hook: the youngest son, out with the sheep, is chosen and anointed
714.howItsDone: Christians read 1 Samuel 16:7 as a reminder that God does not judge by appearance, and read the anointing of the youngest son alongside other stories in scripture where God chooses the overlooked.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mizpeh, where Saul hid among the baggage. Your line was come out from the baggage.

An old prophet is grieving, and God tells him to stop: "How long wilt thou mourn for Saul, seeing I have rejected him from reigning over Israel? fill thine horn with oil, and go." The tall king from yesterday has gone wrong, and Samuel can't let go of him. He's sent to Bethlehem, to Jesse, grandson of Ruth and Boaz. Samuel is afraid: "How can I go? if Saul hear it, he will kill me." So he goes quietly, with a heifer for a sacrifice, and invites Jesse and his sons. One of them is about to be anointed king. Samuel doesn't know which.
screen: `HOW LONG WILT THOU MOURN FOR SAUL?`

segments.voice: Jesse's son Eliab walks in first, and Samuel thinks he's found him: "Surely the LORD'S anointed is before him." God answers with the line that names today: "Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart." Yesterday the crowd cheered a king taller than everyone from the shoulders up. Samuel is about to be drawn by height again, and God stops him. The sons pass by: "Jesse made seven of his sons to pass before Samuel. And Samuel said unto Jesse, The LORD hath not chosen these." Then: "Are here all thy children?" Jesse admits, "There remaineth yet the youngest, and, behold, he keepeth the sheep." Nobody thought to call him in. Samuel says, we will not sit down till he comes. Until now, the story hasn't said his name. He arrives, and the text, with a little smile, describes him anyway: "ruddy, and withal of a beautiful countenance, and goodly to look to." The point was never that looks are bad. It's that they aren't what God goes by. "Arise, anoint him: for this is he." Samuel pours the oil in front of his brothers, and only then does the name appear: "the Spirit of the LORD came upon David from that day forward." Samuel goes home to Ramah. Nothing in these verses makes the boy king yet.
screen: `SURELY THE LORD'S ANOINTED IS BEFORE HIM.`

segments.voice: Think of one person you've sized up by the outside, their clothes, age, accent, job, the way they talk: someone you'd have left out with the sheep. Hold their face for a moment and try to look past it: what do you actually know of their heart? If you pray, ask to see them the way the text says God sees.
Eliab. Jesse's eldest son, whom Samuel almost anointed before God said, man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart.
